strengths: Synth-SBDH addresses a concrete clinical NLP resource gap: 8,767 synthetic examples provide spans, presence, temporality, and rationales across 15 categories. Its public availability reduces dependence on restricted clinical corpora.

The experiments convincingly demonstrate utility for smaller classification models. On MIMIC-SBDH, prompt-based RoBERTa improves from 55.64 to 91.11 macro F, with improvements also observed under standard fine-tuning. Multiple model families, two clinical sources, three independent runs, and training-size ablations provide substantial supporting evidence.

Expert review of all 1,755 synthetic test examples, adjudication, corrected rationales, and detailed error analysis are valuable investments in dataset quality. The generation prompts, 45 seed examples, annotation guidelines, training configurations, and reported data/checkpoint release support reproducibility.
The resource and demonstrated classification benefits constitute a contribution suitable for Findings. Its publication value does not depend on introducing a new generation algorithm.
weaknesses: The claim of consistently improved performance is broader than the results support. Table 4 shows essentially unchanged encoder NER performance, while the large T5 improvement starts from an unusually unstable baseline. Table 14 shows negligible or negative gains for Llama models. The striking housing result also relies on only 18 positive test examples; variability across training seeds does not capture uncertainty from this small evaluation sample.

Baseline reporting needs clarification. Sections D.1 and D.2 both reference Table 13, but interpret its comparison as ordinary downstream training versus synthetic pretraining and as MIMIC pretraining versus synthetic pretraining, respectively. The table does not separately identify these conditions. Class-weighting or oversampling controls would also help establish whether the rare-category gains exceed simpler approaches to imbalance.

The benchmark-quality assessment has methodological limitations. Experts reviewed visible GPT-4 annotations, and Appendix E.2 explicitly allows retaining an ambiguous category that would be assigned differently when adding a missing annotation. This makes the reference labels partly dependent on GPT-4's initial choices. Furthermore, human agreement includes missing annotations whereas LLM self-evaluation excludes them, so their alignment percentages are not directly comparable. A blind annotation subset under a consistent policy would strengthen the benchmark claim.

Evidence for rationale distillation is modest: Table 5 reports gains of 0.66 and 0.58 macro-F points, with the latter nonsignificant, exclusively on synthetic test data. These results support a possible auxiliary-supervision benefit but do not establish transferred reasoning capability. The experiments also leave temporal prediction and explicit negated-span extraction unevaluated despite these being distinctive dataset attributes.

The statistical testing procedure and unit of analysis are insufficiently specified. In particular, the reported p<0.001 for T5 NER needs explanation given three runs and a baseline macro-F standard deviation of 18.24. Reproducible test details and confidence intervals would make the significance claims assessable.

External validity and independent replication remain limited. Examples average only 13.7 words and originate from a small set of VHA-inspired seeds; the real-data experiments establish utility with supervised target-domain adaptation. The private VA dataset also prevents unrestricted reproduction of the real-world NER and training-size results. These limitations constrain the broader generalizability claim.
